questions.q: How does “Neo-Gandhism,” as the editorial describes it, differ from the Gandhian method used before 1947?
options: It seeks help from foreign powers
Not quite. The article says: It works by re-educating minds, where the older method relied on mass mobilization.
It gives up Gandhi’s ideas altogether
Not quite. The article says: It works by re-educating minds, where the older method relied on mass mobilization.
It allows force where peaceful protest fails
Not quite. The article says: It works by re-educating minds, where the older method relied on mass mobilization.
It works by re-educating minds, where the older method relied on mass mobilization
Yes. “Mob activism” is to be replaced by “educational activism.”
questions.rationale: “While the old pattern of the Gandhian method was based on mass mobilization, Neo-Gandhism will be based on the re-engineering of people’s minds.”

questions.q: Why, according to the editorial, have protest methods lost their relevance in India today?
options: The freedom struggle was never truly peaceful
Not quite. The article says: There is no foreign “they” any more – the task is to build one’s own nation, a “we-we” equation.
People have lost interest in public life
Not quite. The article says: There is no foreign “they” any more – the task is to build one’s own nation, a “we-we” equation.
Protests are now forbidden by law
Not quite. The article says: There is no foreign “they” any more – the task is to build one’s own nation, a “we-we” equation.
There is no foreign “they” any more – the task is to build one’s own nation, a “we-we” equation
Exactly. The target is now ourselves.
questions.rationale: “Now, there is no ‘they’; all are members of the Indian nation. The present situation is based on a ‘we-we’ equation, and not a ‘we-they’ equation as it was in the past.”

questions.q: Astronaut James Irwin felt God’s presence on the moon. Why, says the article, do most of us not feel it on earth?
options: Only a few chosen people can feel it
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity – we have seen the world’s wonders since childhood and take them for granted.
The earth is less wonderful than the moon
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity – we have seen the world’s wonders since childhood and take them for granted.
Modern life leaves no time for nature
Not quite. The article says: Familiarity – we have seen the world’s wonders since childhood and take them for granted.
Familiarity – we have seen the world’s wonders since childhood and take them for granted
Right. We must look “as if we are seeing them for the first time.”
questions.rationale: “By observing the world around us from an early age, we become accustomed to it; we take it so much for granted that we fail to perceive its uniqueness.”

questions.q: A Delhi street vendor was given cloth worth Rs 150,000 on credit. What had earned him this?
options: Years of paying his debts before they were due
Yes. Trust is built by acting, not by claiming to be trustworthy.
His skill at persuading people
Not quite. The article says: Years of paying his debts before they were due.
A large cash deposit
Not quite. The article says: Years of paying his debts before they were due.
A relative’s guarantee
Not quite. The article says: Years of paying his debts before they were due.
questions.rationale: “The way to establish trust is not by repeating how trustworthy one is. No, it is by acting in a trustworthy manner… consistently… over a long period.”

questions.q: What, according to the article, was the real conflict that made science seem opposed to religion?
options: A conflict between Newton and the Church
Not quite. The article says: A conflict between science and an old theology built on Greek and Egyptian philosophy.
A conflict between science and an old theology built on Greek and Egyptian philosophy
Well done. It was not divine religion that science contradicted.
A conflict between scientists of different countries
Not quite. The article says: A conflict between science and an old theology built on Greek and Egyptian philosophy.
A conflict between Darwin’s followers and Newton’s
Not quite. The article says: A conflict between science and an old theology built on Greek and Egyptian philosophy.
questions.rationale: “It was, in fact, a conflict between science and ancient theology, which had been founded on Greek and Egyptian philosophy rather than on divine religion.”

questions.q: The article says every real achievement takes “fifteen years.” What point is it making?
options: Businesses should be sold after fifteen years
Not quite. The article says: Lasting success comes only through long, continuous effort, in line with the laws God has set.
Young people should not begin anything early
Not quite. The article says: Lasting success comes only through long, continuous effort, in line with the laws God has set.
Lasting success comes only through long, continuous effort, in line with the laws God has set
Exactly. Instant success is called an illusion.
Fifteen is a number with special meaning
Not quite. The article says: Lasting success comes only through long, continuous effort, in line with the laws God has set.
questions.rationale: “Those who long for a recipe for instant success are, in fact, living in a fool’s paradise… The only condition to succeed is continuous effort.”

questions.q: How did Mahatma Gandhi’s early shyness turn to his advantage?
options: It won him the sympathy of judges
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that he rarely spoke or wrote thoughtlessly.
It kept him out of politics until he was ready
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that he rarely spoke or wrote thoughtlessly.
It taught him economy of words, so that he rarely spoke or wrote thoughtlessly
Yes. He called his hesitancy “now a pleasure.”
It led him to take up writing instead of law
Not quite. The article says: It taught him economy of words, so that he rarely spoke or wrote thoughtlessly.
questions.rationale: Gandhi wrote: “Its greatest benefit has been that it has taught me the economy of words… a thoughtless word hardly ever escaped my tongue or pen.”

questions.q: When one side argues calmly with reasons and the other answers with mockery, what does the article say this shows?
options: That the calm speaker lacks conviction
Not quite. The article says: That the one who reasons is in the right.
That the one who reasons is in the right
Correct. The Prophets spoke the language of reason.
That the matter cannot be settled
Not quite. The article says: That the one who reasons is in the right.
That both sides are equally unsure
Not quite. The article says: That the one who reasons is in the right.
questions.rationale: “This difference in approach is a sure indication that the former is in the right and his opponents are in the wrong.”

questions.q: What is “the lesson that the platform teaches” the passenger who missed his train?
options: It is better to travel by another route
Not quite. The article says: There is always a next train – a second opportunity to be patiently awaited and taken.
A missed chance never returns
Not quite. The article says: There is always a next train – a second opportunity to be patiently awaited and taken.
One should always arrive early
Not quite. The article says: There is always a next train – a second opportunity to be patiently awaited and taken.
There is always a next train – a second opportunity to be patiently awaited and taken
Right. Blaming others only wastes energy.
questions.rationale: “There is always that ‘next train’ for them to catch… being ready to avail of that God-given second opportunity.”

questions.q: How, according to the article, would remembering death change the way a person treats others?
options: He would see no sense in oppressing others or in pride, since he must soon come under the will of Another
Yes. Greatness that does not last has no value.
He would hurry to enjoy what he has
Not quite. The article says: He would see no sense in oppressing others or in pride, since he must soon come under the will of Another.
He would stop making any plans
Not quite. The article says: He would see no sense in oppressing others or in pride, since he must soon come under the will of Another.
He would withdraw from people altogether
Not quite. The article says: He would see no sense in oppressing others or in pride, since he must soon come under the will of Another.
questions.rationale: “He would realize that it is fruitless to oppress others if tomorrow he would have to come under the control of Another.”
